definition: unable to be appeased or calmed; relentless
memoryTip: Im-placable: cannot be placated — nothing soothes that anger.
correctPassage: An implacable foe of the treaty refused every compromise offered at the table.
wrongPassages: The judge was implacable once she accepted both sides' settlement terms.
His implacable apology ended the dispute before anyone raised a voice.
She stayed implacable toward the puppy that had chewed her shoes.

definition: harmful or hostile; unfriendly
memoryTip: Enemy-ical — like an enemy: harmful or unfriendly.
correctPassage: Conditions on the planet's surface are inimical to known forms of life.
wrongPassages: The warm climate proved inimical to the citrus groves that thrived there.
Her inimical welcome included fresh towels and a basket of fruit.
They called the mentoring program inimical because every intern found a job.

definition: attribute a quality or fault to someone
memoryTip: Im-pute: put the blame (or a quality) onto someone.
correctPassage: It is unfair to impute bad motives when the evidence is still incomplete.
wrongPassages: She hoped to impute the missing file by downloading it again from the server.
The clerk will impute the receipt into the scanner before you leave.
They tried to impute the fence so the neighbors could not see the yard.

definition: holding firmly; persistent
memoryTip: Tenax = holding tight — a grip that will not let go.
correctPassage: Tenacious reporting eventually uncovered the source of the leak.
wrongPassages: His tenacious interest faded after the first page of the novel.
She gave a tenacious shrug and walked away from the unfinished project.
The tenacious soft ice cream melted before anyone could take a bite.

definition: producing a beneficial effect
memoryTip: Salute to health — good for you, even when the lesson is harsh.
correctPassage: The failure had a salutary effect: teams began documenting assumptions.
wrongPassages: Skipping every practice session had a salutary effect on her performance.
The salutary mold behind the sink spread into the drywall overnight.
Voters called the tax hike salutary only because it funded nothing useful.

definition: giving a false or misleading impression
memoryTip: Delusion-ive — creates a false belief that feels true.
correctPassage: The hope of a quick fix proved delusive once costs doubled.
wrongPassages: Her delusive notes matched the lecture word for word on every slide.
The map was delusive because every landmark sat exactly where it claimed.
They trusted the delusive receipt that correctly listed each item and price.

definition: full of twists and turns; overly complex
memoryTip: A tortured path — winding twists, or an argument that never ends.
correctPassage: A tortuous legal path delayed the project for years.
wrongPassages: The highway ran in a tortuous straight line across the empty plain.
Her tortuous summary fit the entire case on a single index card.
He preferred the tortuous staircase that climbed in one unbroken flight.

definition: attempting to avoid notice; secretive
memoryTip: Fur-tive like a thief's quiet sneak — a secretive glance.
correctPassage: He cast a furtive glance at the clock during the interview.
wrongPassages: Her furtive announcement ran as a full-page ad in the morning paper.
The band made a furtive entrance with fireworks and a marching parade.
He gave a furtive keynote from the main stage under bright spotlights.

definition: expose the falseness of a claim or idea
memoryTip: De-bunk: knock the bunk (nonsense) out — prove it false.
correctPassage: The article seeks to debunk popular myths about human memory.
wrongPassages: She hoped to debunk the broken chair by gluing the leg back on.
The chef will debunk the soup with salt before serving it.
They tried to debunk the celebration by ordering an even larger cake.

definition: a distinctive feature or sign of quality
memoryTip: Gold hallmark stamp — the distinctive mark of real quality.
correctPassage: Clarity is the hallmark of her scientific writing.
wrongPassages: Confusion is the hallmark of her carefully organized lab notebook.
They called silence the hallmark of the stadium during the championship roar.
Random typos became the hallmark of the carefully proofread final draft.

definition: able to be exchanged without changing the result
memoryTip: Inter-change — swap them and nothing really changes.
correctPassage: In this model the two variables are not interchangeable.
wrongPassages: The one-of-a-kind signed manuscript was interchangeable with any unsigned reprint.
His unique fingerprint was interchangeable with everyone else in the database.
The locked password and the public welcome sign proved fully interchangeable.

definition: express the essential features of something briefly
memoryTip: In a capsule — sum up the essence in a tight package.
correctPassage: One sentence can rarely encapsulate a decade of research.
wrongPassages: She tried to encapsulate the rumor by posting an unconfirmed theory online.
He moved to encapsulate the deposition by claiming the audio was corrupted.
They hoped to encapsulate the boycott with influencer posts and no policy changes.

definition: treating a serious matter with deliberate, often inappropriate humor
memoryTip: Facet + joking face — treating serious things lightly on purpose.
correctPassage: A facetious remark during the briefing was widely misread as policy.
wrongPassages: Her facetious eulogy never once broke into a smile or a joke.
The surgeon kept a facetious silence while explaining the risks of the procedure.
He filed a facetious tax return that listed every income source in careful detail.

definition: hidden from view; private and not often visited
memoryTip: Se-clude: shut away — private and hard to reach.
correctPassage: The cabin sits in a secluded valley far from any road.
wrongPassages: The secluded plaza hosted a street fair with food trucks every weekend.
Her secluded desk sat in the center of the open office under bright lights.
They chose a secluded table next to the host stand at the crowded entrance.

definition: get or bring something back
memoryTip: Re-trieve: bring it back (like a retriever dog).
correctPassage: Software can retrieve deleted files for a limited time.
wrongPassages: She hoped to retrieve the email by typing a brand-new message from scratch.
They tried to retrieve the meeting by canceling it before anyone arrived.
He will retrieve the broken vase by leaving the shards on the floor.

definition: make look or feel younger, fresher, or more vital
memoryTip: Re-juvenile: make young or fresh again.
correctPassage: A new arts festival helped rejuvenate the downtown district.
wrongPassages: They hoped to rejuvenate the garden by paving every bed with concrete.
Skipping sleep and meals will rejuvenate anyone before a long exam week.
The factory planned to rejuvenate the river by dumping untreated waste into it.

definition: difficult to understand
memoryTip: Abstract + obtuse difficulty — hard for most people to grasp.
correctPassage: The proof is abstruse even for specialists in the field.
wrongPassages: Her abstruse briefing covered risks, costs, and a clear next step in four slides.
The abstruse picture book used only three-word sentences and bright photos.
He called the fire-exit map abstruse because arrows pointed the only way out.

definition: aggressive and ready to fight
memoryTip: Belli = war — speech or manner that is eager to fight.
correctPassage: Bellicose rhetoric made a diplomatic solution harder to reach.
wrongPassages: Her bellicose reply thanked everyone and offered to reschedule the meeting.
The bellicose treaty banned weapons and created a permanent peace commission.
He gave a bellicose hug to the rival coach after the final whistle.

definition: a harsh, jarring mixture of sounds
memoryTip: Caco (bad) + phony (sound) — a harsh clash of noise.
correctPassage: A cacophony of car horns filled the street at rush hour.
wrongPassages: The gallery's cacophony hang placed one quiet work per wall with wide margins.
Listeners praised the choir's cacophony for its perfect blend and soft dynamics.
The library enforced a strict cacophony so only whispers could be heard.

definition: causing harm or damage
memoryTip: Delete-erious: deletes health — harmful in effect.
correctPassage: Even low levels of the chemical may have deleterious effects.
wrongPassages: The doctor called the vaccine deleterious because side effects were rare and mild.
Fresh air and sleep had a deleterious effect on her energy after the flu.
They praised the safety rails for their deleterious impact on accident rates.
